segment_name: A Mill Town Awakening: North and South's First Collision

questions.question: Caroline, you've described Margaret's first encounter with Milton as almost a physical recoil — like her body understands something her brain is refusing to process. Can you read us the passage you've got marked and walk us through what Gaskell is actually doing there? Because I want to nail down what you mean when you say it builds dread and fascination at the same time — those feel like opposite things.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the first visual impression passage aloud and articulate the core tension in Gaskell's sensory prose; sets up her 'snobbery on display' argument for Margaret's character

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on something you said before we started recording — that Gaskell's real radical move isn't what she shows us but how she structures the showing. Because Caroline just talked about Margaret's emotional recoil, and James is going to tell us this is all about contract law and capital. But you're saying it's the *syntax*? Can you find me a sentence — just one — where the form of the sentence is actually the argument?
questions.intent: Force Eleanor to demonstrate her formal/structural claim concretely with a specific textual example; creates a productive three-way tension between emotional, formal, and political readings

questions.question: James, you've called this novel 'legal realism avant la lettre' and I love that phrase but I want to stress-test it. When Margaret first meets the mill owners — when wages get explained to her like arithmetic — what exactly is Gaskell documenting? Because Caroline would say Margaret's moral discomfort is the point, Eleanor would say it's the fractured prose around that moment, and you're saying neither of those things. What are you actually seeing that they're missing?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's strongest institutional critique and force a direct confrontation with the other two readings; the 'what are you seeing that they're missing' framing should provoke Caroline and Eleanor to defend their positions

questions.question: Caroline, I need to bring you back in here because you said before we started that you'd push back hard on the idea that these opening pages are in any way 'balanced' — that Gaskell is actually doing something more uncomfortable and deliberate with Margaret. James has just argued the real story is institutional. Eleanor's in the prose architecture. But your strongest claim is that readers who let Margaret off the hook for her early snobbery miss the whole novel. So where exactly does Gaskell catch her in the act — is there a specific exchange you'd want us to hear?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read a Margaret dialogue passage that shows her prejudice in real time; sets up a three-way argument about whether the novel's engine is individual moral failure, formal technique, or structural injustice

questions.question: Eleanor, last question for this segment and I want you to settle something — James thinks Gaskell is furious about institutions and precise about it, Caroline thinks she's precise about individual moral hypocrisy. You've said the novel's modern sensibility lives in the moments where Gaskell *withholds* understanding, leaves Margaret and us genuinely confused. Is that actually a political position, or is it a formal one? Because I'm not sure those are the same thing.
questions.intent: Force Eleanor to resolve or productively refuse to resolve the tension between her formalist reading and the political stakes the other two experts have raised; good closing provocation that should pull all three into the same thread

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that's genuinely productive: Caroline reads emotionally and morally, Eleanor reads formally and structurally, James reads institutionally and politically. Don't let any one frame dominate too early — the goal is to keep all three in conversation until the final question. Push for concrete textual moments whenever an expert goes abstract; the passages are the anchor. Watch for James and Caroline talking past each other on the individual vs. institutional question — that's the live wire in this segment. If energy dips, ask someone to just read a sentence aloud and react to it.
cross_engagement_targets: James Blackstone's 'legal realism' framing directly challenges Caroline's focus on Margaret's individual moral journey — Caroline should be invited to respond to whether institutional critique and personal moral growth can coexist in the same reading, or whether one swallows the other.

Eleanor Hartley's claim that form IS meaning collides with Blackstone's argument that the content of Gaskell's social documentation is doing the heavy lifting — push them to argue directly about whether you can separate what Gaskell writes from how she writes it.

Caroline's insistence that the opening pages are 'deliberately disorienting, not balanced' is a direct counter to what Eleanor identifies as Gaskell's 'deceptively restrained' technique — these sound similar but may be arguing for opposite effects; surface this explicitly.

segment_name: The Architecture of a Novel: How Gaskell Builds Sympathy

questions.question: Eleanor, you talked before we started about Gaskell doing something sneaky with her narrator — pulling the rug out from under us at key moments. Can you show us what you mean? Is there a passage where you can actually hear her doing that?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read a passage and demonstrate the limited-narrator technique, establishing the formal craft argument early — and immediately giving James and Caroline something to respond to

questions.question: James, I want to push you on something. Eleanor's just shown us Gaskell doing this very precise, controlled narrative thing — and your argument, as I understand it, is that the real power is in the institutional mechanics, the wages, the actual arithmetic of poverty. But can those two things coexist? Or does the formal cleverness actually get in the way of the structural critique?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement with Eleanor's point — Blackstone's instinct will be to downplay formal craft in favour of economic structure, which should provoke both Eleanor and Caroline

questions.question: Caroline, you used a phrase I've been thinking about — 'enforced intimacy.' You said Gaskell puts you inside someone at their most vulnerable and then refuses to let you judge them. I wonder if James would say that's actually a problem — that making us feel for individuals is precisely what lets us off the hook from the systemic critique. What do you say to that?
questions.intent: Set up the sharpest disagreement in the room: emotional-acoustic sympathy versus structural-political sympathy — get Caroline to defend interiority against Blackstone's institutional reading

questions.question: James, there's a moment — I think it's in the wage negotiation scenes — where Thornton has to essentially admit he cannot fully understand what it costs to be one of his workers. You mentioned that before. Read us that bit, because I want to know: is that Gaskell being honest about the limits of sympathy, or is it a cop-out?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to read the mutual-incomprehension passage and argue for unresolved tension as the novel's true position — directly challenges anyone who wants a tidier reading

questions.question: Last one — and I want everyone in on this. Caroline, you said you can reread this book at seventeen and forty and cry each time. But here's my question: is that a sign of how good the novel is, or is it actually Gaskell's trap? Does making us feel so much for Margaret let the mill-owners — let the whole system — quietly off the hook?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the central tension unresolved: does emotional architecture serve or undermine political clarity? Should produce genuine three-way disagreement and a strong close

steering_notes: This segment has a natural fault line running through it: James wants to talk about economic structures, Eleanor wants to talk about narrative form, and Caroline wants to talk about emotional acoustics — but all three are actually describing the same novel from different angles. The best moments will come when they're forced to acknowledge each other's evidence rather than talk past it. Push back if anyone gets too abstract; keep demanding they go to the text. The 'cop-out' question at the end should be genuinely provocative — let it run.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline's 'enforced intimacy' argument directly contradicts James's worry about sentimentality as a political evasion — he thinks making us feel for individuals obscures the system; she thinks that intimacy IS the system made legible. Get them to argue this explicitly.

Eleanor's limited-narrator point and Caroline's 'acoustic' reading are actually deeply compatible — both are talking about form as the site of meaning. But Eleanor will frame it structurally and Caroline will frame it emotionally. A good moment is to point this out and ask if they're actually saying the same thing.

James's insistence that the novel doesn't resolve its contradictions is a direct challenge to any reading — Eleanor's or Caroline's — that finds craft-satisfaction or emotional catharsis in the ending. Flag this when it comes up: satisfaction and unresolved tension are in tension with each other.

segment_name: Margaret's Reckoning: The Cost of Loyalty and Deception

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that the lie is actually the most honest moment in the book. That feels almost paradoxical. Can you walk us through what you mean by that, and maybe read us the passage where Margaret first commits to the deception?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to lay out her 'deception as integrity' reading in full, open the emotional register for the segment, and get the key passage read aloud early so everyone has the text in their heads

questions.question: James, I suspect you heard Caroline just now and thought — that's a generous reading. You've been pretty insistent that this moment isn't just about Margaret's heart, it's about what the law would do to someone else in the same position. Can you put that argument on the table? Who's actually protected when Margaret lies?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement with Caroline's sympathetic reading by bringing in the class asymmetry argument — Margaret's 'integrity' has a very particular price tag depending on who's paying it

questions.question: Eleanor, you've been listening to this and I notice you've got a different angle entirely — you're not as interested in whether the lie is right or wrong, you're interested in what it does to Margaret's body. There's a passage you wanted to read about her face or her throat giving her away before she can stop it. Let's hear it — because I think it might actually cut through this disagreement.
questions.intent: Introduce Eleanor's somatic reading as a kind of third way that neither vindicates nor condemns Margaret but shows Gaskell doing something technically remarkable — also gets the key physical passage read aloud

questions.question: Here's what I want to push on, Eleanor — you said Margaret doesn't really choose the deception, it almost chooses her. But Caroline thinks she's finally acting from her own heart, and James thinks she knows exactly what she's doing and who it benefits. Can all three of those things be true at once, or does one of them have to give?
questions.intent: Force a three-way collision on the question of Margaret's agency — is she instinctive, deliberate, or complicit — and see if the experts can find common ground or sharpen their disagreements

questions.question: James, last word on this — you said Margaret gets to agonize in private while a mill worker in the same position goes to prison. Does Gaskell know that? Is the novel actually critiquing Margaret, or is it so deep inside her perspective that it can't see it?
questions.intent: End the segment on the sharpest possible version of the class question — forces James to commit to whether this is a flaw or a feature of the novel, and gives Caroline and Eleanor a chance to defend Gaskell

steering_notes: This segment has real heat in it — Caroline and James are going to disagree almost immediately and that's good, let it run. The risk is that the class argument and the emotional argument talk past each other without ever engaging. Your job is to force them to address the same question: not 'is Margaret right or wrong' but 'what does Gaskell think she's doing here and does the novel know more than Margaret does?' Eleanor is the wild card — her somatic reading can either bridge the other two or complicate them further. Use her as a reset valve if the Caroline-James argument gets circular. Make sure at least two passages get read aloud — the lie itself and one of Eleanor's body-language moments. The text needs to be in the room.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline says the deception IS the integrity — James says that integrity is a class luxury. These positions need to be in the same sentence. Ask Caroline directly: does her reading only work because Margaret can afford for it to work?

Eleanor believes Margaret doesn't choose the lie so much as fall into it — Caroline thinks this is the first moment Margaret acts as a fully autonomous agent. This is a direct contradiction about what kind of heroine Margaret is and neither panelist has addressed the other's version yet.

James argues the novel understands Margaret's complicity more clearly than Margaret does — Eleanor would say Gaskell doesn't resolve it through moral logic at all but through bodily suffering. These could be complementary but neither has acknowledged it — push them to find out if they're actually agreeing about Gaskell's method while disagreeing about her politics.

segment_name: Factory and Fury: Thornton, Higgins, and the Strike

questions.question: Caroline, you've said something that I keep coming back to — that if you read this novel *aloud*, you literally can't reduce these men to ideology. Can you pick a passage right now and show us what you mean? Because that's a bold claim and I want to hear it.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read aloud and demonstrate her 'verbal music' argument — creates an immediate, sensory anchor for the whole conversation and lets the text do work early

questions.question: Eleanor, you've called Gaskell's refusal to resolve the class conflict *radical* — that she deliberately keeps us off-balance. But James would probably say that's not a formal choice, that's just how industrial conflict actually worked: nobody won, everybody was scared, and the law stayed broken. Is there a difference between Gaskell being formally radical and Gaskell just being historically accurate?
questions.intent: Provoke the core Hartley-Blackstone disagreement — form versus history, aesthetic argument versus institutional argument — as early as possible

questions.question: James, you said something in our chat that genuinely surprised me — that Thornton's evolution isn't really a moral journey, it's more like a man who's seen bodies in the street and done a cold calculation. That's a much darker reading than most people bring to this book. Where in the text does Gaskell actually signal that? Is there a moment where we can see it's pragmatism, not conscience?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's strongest, most unsentimental take and push him to locate it in specific textual evidence — sets up direct conflict with Caroline's more sympathetic reading of Thornton's bewilderment

questions.question: Caroline, James is basically saying Thornton's confusion and vulnerability — the thing you find so poignant — is actually just a man realizing he can't ignore workers anymore because the costs got too high. Does that reading kill what you love about those scenes, or can both things be true at once?
questions.intent: Force direct engagement between Woodcourt's emotional-psychological reading and Blackstone's institutional one — this is the sharpest cross-engagement point in the segment

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on one thing. You've said Gaskell keeps character and principle inseparable in Higgins — that we can't psychologize him, that he *is* his ideology in some sense. But doesn't that risk making him a bit of a monument rather than a man? Caroline thinks Gaskell is doing something warmer than that. Who's right about what Higgins actually is on the page?
questions.intent: Surface the Hartley-Woodcourt disagreement about whether Gaskell's formal discipline humanizes or flattens Higgins — get them to argue directly about the same character

steering_notes: Keep pulling the conversation back to the text whenever the debate gets too abstract — Caroline is the natural anchor here because she wants to read aloud and demonstrate. Let Hartley and Blackstone's form-versus-history argument run hot but don't let it become a seminar; redirect through Caroline's more visceral, performative instincts. The richest moment will probably be the three-way collision over what Thornton's 'transformation' actually is — sentiment, pragmatism, or formal device. Don't resolve it. Let it sit.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley argues Gaskell's discomfort is a *formal* choice; Blackstone argues it's just historical realism — they're making incompatible claims about authorial intention that neither can fully prove, and that tension should be named out loud

Woodcourt reads Thornton's confusion as poignant and humanizing; Blackstone reads it as cold calculation dressed up as feeling — they're looking at the same passages and seeing opposite things, which is itself worth remarking on

Hartley insists Gaskell doesn't let us psychologize Higgins; Woodcourt's whole approach is to get inside how these men *feel* — this is a direct methodological clash that should be surfaced when both are talking about Higgins in the same breath
All three implicitly disagree about whether the novel's ending is resolution, compromise, or ongoing tension — worth a direct three-way question if time allows

segment_name: The Quiet Subversions: Gaskell's Comic Intelligence

questions.question: Caroline, you used the phrase 'moral entrapment' in our chat before the show — which I love — and it made me think: is Gaskell actually playing a trick on the reader? Like, are we laughing and then suddenly realizing we've been caught out?
questions.intent: Open the segment with Caroline's sharpest take on reader complicity, set up the 'what is this comedy actually *doing*' question that all three will have different answers to

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on something — because Caroline's framing makes Gaskell sound almost cold, like she's setting a trap. But you've talked about dramatic irony as *tenderness*. Can those two things coexist? Is she trapping us warmly, or is there something more uncomfortable going on?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement with Caroline's 'entrapment' framing versus Eleanor's more generous reading, expose the real tension between them — gentle satirist vs. forensic anatomist

questions.question: James, I have to bring you in here because you'd probably say both Caroline and Eleanor are underselling how *dangerous* this comedy actually was in 1855. Like — Gaskell couldn't just print 'the factory owners are lying to themselves.' So is the humor essentially a legal workaround? A way of saying the unsayable?
questions.intent: Introduce the political-structural reading and provoke the question of whether comedy is form-as-disguise or whether that undersells its aesthetic achievement — Eleanor in particular should want to push back here

questions.question: Eleanor, I know you want to get to a specific passage — the strike negotiations, where Margaret's watching both sides perform their own self-righteousness at the same time. Can you read us a bit of it? Because I think that might be where all three of your readings are actually happening simultaneously.
questions.intent: Get a passage read aloud, ground the abstract discussion in the text, and create a moment where all three experts can stake out territory on the same lines — high cross-engagement potential

questions.question: Last one — and this is the one I can't stop thinking about. All three of you have suggested Gaskell is doing something technically extraordinary with comic voice. But she's also writing in the shadow of Austen, who did this first. So is Gaskell extending what Austen figured out, or is she doing something genuinely different — maybe darker, maybe more political? Where does she depart?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the legacy question that forces all three to synthesize their readings and commit to a position on Gaskell's place in the tradition — designed to produce a three-way disagreement with real stakes

steering_notes: The core tension to cultivate: Eleanor sees the comedy as structurally generous and craft-driven; Caroline sees it as morally entrapping and microscopically cruel; James sees it as politically radical in form. These aren't incompatible but each expert will instinctively reach for their framing. Push them to address each other's language directly — get 'entrapment' and 'tenderness' and 'institutional critique' in the same exchange. The passage read-aloud in question 4 is the pivot: use it to move from theory to text and back. Don't let the Austen comparison at the end become a ranking exercise — keep it about what Gaskell is *doing differently* in her historical moment.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline's 'moral entrapment' vs Eleanor's 'dramatic irony as tenderness' — these are the same observation from opposite emotional poles; pressing both on this will produce the segment's best moment

James insists comedy IS the politics; Eleanor insists the comedy transcends its political function into something aesthetically autonomous — this is a direct and productive contradiction worth naming out loud

Caroline thinks Eleanor will read the comedy as broadly satirical toward 'society'; Eleanor actually wants to say it's more structurally sophisticated than that — they may agree more than they expect, which is also interesting radio

James's claim that working-class characters' comic asides are 'the novel's moral compass' is a concrete claim that Caroline and Eleanor can either support or complicate with specific passages — route back to text here

segment_name: Thematic Depths: Love, Labour, and the Nation

questions.question: Caroline, you've said you genuinely can't decide whether Gaskell's faith in feeling and honest relationship is the most moving thing in the book or the most politically naïve. I want to push on that — because those feel like very different novels. Which is it?
questions.intent: Force Caroline off the fence and into a strong position that James can immediately challenge — gets the disagreement going early and sets the terms of the whole segment

questions.question: James, you've said Thornton's conversion is just 'a patch on a fundamentally unjust system.' But Gaskell clearly wants us to feel it as meaningful — she earns it over four hundred pages. Is she naive, or is she doing something more cunning than that?
questions.intent: Get James to articulate whether Gaskell is complicit in her own conservatism or deliberately exposing its limits — draw out the Chartism context and push him toward the passage about masters' absolute legal power

questions.question: Eleanor, you've talked about Gaskell shifting her prose style — going lyrical for emotional intimacy and then snapping back to something colder for commerce and class. Can you actually show us that? Is there a passage where you can hear it happening?
questions.intent: Get a live reading of a passage showing the tonal shift — this is the moment for the mill interior versus intimate conversation contrast — make the formal argument audible rather than abstract

questions.question: James, Caroline would say the politics only land because we experience them through the relationship — through Margaret and Thornton. You'd say that's exactly the problem. But here's what I want to know: does Gaskell agree with Caroline or with you?
questions.intent: Force James to distinguish between what Gaskell intends and what the novel actually does — opens the gap between authorial design and political effect, and invites Caroline and Eleanor to weigh in on whose Gaskell this is

questions.question: Eleanor, James is essentially saying the love plot domesticates the politics — makes systemic injustice feel solvable by two good people getting together. Caroline is saying that's not domestication, that's the whole point. Your argument about narrative architecture suggests the novel refuses to let those two things separate. So who's right — or is Gaskell playing both of them against each other?
questions.intent: Use Eleanor's formal analysis as a synthesis move — invite her to adjudicate the Blackstone-Woodcourt disagreement using prose evidence, ideally ending on a genuinely unresolved tension that leaves the audience with something to argue about

steering_notes: The central fault line here is between James's structural-political reading and Caroline's faith in feeling and relationship — Eleanor's formal argument is the most useful tool for refusing to let either position win cleanly. Push toward that three-way tension rather than letting it collapse into James vs. Caroline. The best radio moment will come if James concedes that Gaskell might be more clear-eyed about the limits of benevolence than the ending suggests, while Caroline holds her ground on why the love story moves us anyway. Eleanor should be used to ground abstract arguments in specific prose — keep asking for the passage, keep asking what the sentence is actually doing. If the conversation drifts toward Victorian sociology, bring it back to the text. The question 'does the novel solve the problem it sets up?' should be lurking under everything.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline's 'most moving or most politically naïve' undecidability is a direct invitation for James to say it's naïve — get him to say it plainly and let Caroline respond
James's line about 'redemptive for whom — the workers don't marry their way to justice' should be put directly to Caroline, who has to either defend the love plot's politics or concede its limits

Eleanor's claim that Gaskell's formal choices enact the conflict between capitalism and love rather than just describing it is a potential bridge between James and Caroline — use it to ask whether the novel's form is more radical than its ending

James's Chartism context — that working-class political organisation was being violently suppressed while Gaskell was writing — should be introduced as a challenge to any reading that treats the ending as straightforwardly hopeful, including Eleanor's architectural reading

segment_name: Belonging and Becoming: The Novel's Final Gift

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that's been stuck in my head — that Gaskell hands us a Margaret who's still uncertain, still mid-thought, at the very end. But I want to push on that a little. Is that genuinely radical for a Victorian novel, or is it just... the ending Gaskell couldn't quite write her way out of? Like, is the openness a choice or a limitation?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to make the strongest case for deliberate ambiguity as artistic gift, while opening the door for Blackstone to argue it's actually politically purposeful rather than aesthetically unresolved

questions.question: Eleanor, you wanted to read us the exact moment where Gaskell puts Margaret and Thornton in the same space without explaining it — without the narrator stepping in to reassure us. Can you find that passage and read it? And then tell me: what does Gaskell's sentence structure actually do there? Because you mentioned something about the phrasing getting shorter, more fragmented — I want to hear that.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the passage aloud and make the close-reading case for musical tension and structural ambiguity; gives Blackstone a concrete text to redirect toward political reading and Woodcourt to respond on emotional truth

questions.question: James, Eleanor just read us that passage and she's calling it ambiguous, unsettled, almost musical in its restraint. But I remember you saying something pretty different in our chat — you said the ending is fundamentally *political*, that what matters isn't the emotional texture but the fact that Margaret is now an agent inside the industrial world she once despised. So who's right? Is that passage about feeling, or is it about power?
questions.intent: Directly set up the Hartley-Blackstone disagreement; get Blackstone to make the case that the romantic-aesthetic reading actually depoliticises the ending; force the question of whether the two readings are compatible or mutually exclusive

questions.question: Let's test that reading, though. Because the novel is called *North and South*, not *Margaret Hale and the Industrial Question*. If this is really a story about a woman becoming a radical, about class structures having to break down — why does it end with a marriage proposal? Isn't Gaskell giving the conventional ending with one hand while taking it away with the other?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to defend the political reading against the obvious counter — that the marriage plot swallows the radicalism — and create space for Woodcourt to complicate it and Hartley to reframe what 'belonging' actually means structurally

questions.question: Here's what I want to put to all three of you, but Caroline I'll start with you: by the end of the novel, does Margaret *belong* anywhere? Like, genuinely — does she have a home? Or has Gaskell written her into a kind of permanent in-between, and we're supposed to feel that as a gift rather than a loss?
questions.intent: Close the segment by forcing all three experts to commit to a position on the novel's central question; designed to surface the three-way disagreement cleanly — Hartley's 'permanent negotiation', Blackstone's 'she builds a new order', Woodcourt's 'uncertainty as the point' — and give the segment a genuine ending debate

steering_notes: This segment has the richest three-way tension of the lot. The core fault line is: is the ending's openness primarily aesthetic (Hartley), political (Blackstone), or emotional (Woodcourt)? These aren't incompatible but the experts will instinctively defend their lane. Your job is to keep forcing them to respond to each other's *specific* readings rather than talk past each other. The passage-reading in Q2 is the anchor — once Eleanor reads it aloud, the other two have a shared text to fight over, which is much better radio than abstract position-stating. Watch for Blackstone trying to dismiss the romantic reading too quickly; push him to sit with the text before pivoting to politics. Also watch for Hartley and Woodcourt agreeing too comfortably on 'ambiguity' — they actually mean different things by it and that disagreement is worth drawing out. End on the belonging question because it forces a commit.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that the ending is 'a woman becoming a radical' directly challenges Hartley's reading of it as structurally unresolved — Hartley will want to say radicalism and irresolution aren't opposites; push them to argue this out explicitly rather than talking around it

Woodcourt says Margaret's becoming is *despite* Victorian constraints; Hartley says Gaskell structures those constraints permanently into Margaret's character — these are almost opposite readings of whether the novel is ultimately liberating or tragic, and neither expert has clocked that the other is saying something incompatible

Blackstone insists growth is inseparable from Margaret's changed economic position; Woodcourt insists it's about learning to see complexity in people — this is the political vs personal axis, and it maps onto a real debate about what Victorian novels are *for*. Worth surfacing directly if the segment finds energy there
